theory.intro: The index laws you met with numbers work the same way with pronumerals, because $x^{5}$ still means $x$ multiplied by itself $5$ times. The new skill is deciding which law an expression needs. Division requires a nonzero denominator, and expressions with algebraic indices are used only where they are defined.
facts: $a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$ — multiplying powers of the same base **adds** the indices.
$a^{m}\div a^{n}=a^{m-n}$ — dividing powers of the same base **subtracts** the indices.
A fraction bar means division, so $\frac{a^{m}}{a^{n}}=a^{m-n}$ as well.
When the **denominator** has the higher power, take the difference of the indices and leave the base underneath: $\frac{x^{2}}{x^{7}}=\frac{1}{x^{5}}$.
$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n}=a^{m\times n}$ — a power of a power **multiplies** the indices.
A pronumeral written with no index has index $1$: $w^{4}\times w=w^{4}\times w^{1}=w^{5}$.
The laws only apply when the **bases match**, so $x^{5}\times y^{2}$ and $\frac{g^{7}}{m^{4}}$ cannot be simplified.
Adding two powers is collecting like terms, not an index law: $h^{2}+h^{2}=2h^{2}$.
steps: Check that the bases are the same.
Decide which law applies — multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them, a power of a power multiplies them.
Apply the law to the indices and write the result as a single power, or as a reciprocal with a positive index when the denominator has the higher power.

workedExamples.question_text: Write $t^{3}\times t^{6}\times t$ as a single power.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Add the indices of matching bases. The final $t$ has index $1$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}t^{3}\times t^{6}\times t\\&=t^{3+6+1}\\&=t^{10}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Explain why $u^{4}\times v^{3}$ and $\frac{u^{8}}{v^{2}}$ cannot be simplified using the multiplication or division index laws.
workedExamples.solution_text: Each expression has different bases, $u$ and $v$. These index laws require matching bases. The product can be written as $u^{4}v^{3}$; the fraction stays $\frac{u^{8}}{v^{2}}$.

workedExamples.question_text: Write $\frac{h^{10}}{h}$ as a single power, where $h\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
A fraction bar means division. Subtract the denominator's index, including the implied index $1$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{h^{10}}{h}\\&=h^{10-1}\\&=h^{9}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Simplify $\frac{c^{3}}{c^{8}}$, using a positive index, where $c\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The denominator has the higher power, so leave the base underneath and take the difference of the indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{c^{3}}{c^{8}}\\&=\frac{1}{c^{8-3}}\\&=\frac{1}{c^{5}}\end{aligned}$

A power of a power multiplies the indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}(k^{4})^{3}\\&=k^{4\times3}\\&=k^{12}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: State whether to add or multiply the indices, then simplify each expression: (a) $s^{5}\times s^{3}$; (b) $(s^{5})^{3}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Two powers of the same base are multiplied, so add the indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}s^{5}\times s^{3}\\&=s^{5+3}\\&=s^{8}\end{aligned}$
(b) A power is raised to another power, so multiply the indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}(s^{5})^{3}\\&=s^{5\times3}\\&=s^{15}\end{aligned}$

In the first fraction, the denominator has the higher power.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{r^{6}}{r^{13}}\\&=\frac{1}{r^{13-6}}\\&=\frac{1}{r^{7}}\end{aligned}$
In the second fraction, the numerator has the higher power.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{r^{13}}{r^{6}}\\&=r^{13-6}\\&=r^{7}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Write $\frac{(z^{2})^{5}\times z^{4}}{(z^{3})^{2}}$ as a single power, where $z\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Simplify the powers of powers first, then combine the product and quotient.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{(z^{2})^{5}\times z^{4}}{(z^{3})^{2}}\\&=\frac{z^{10}\times z^{4}}{z^{6}}\\&=\frac{z^{14}}{z^{6}}\\&=z^{14-6}\\&=z^{8}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A student writes $f^{5}\times f^{2}=f^{10}$ and $f^{9}\div f^{3}=1^{3}$. Explain each error and give the correct answers, where $f\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
For multiplication, add the indices rather than multiplying them.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}f^{5}\times f^{2}\\&=f^{5+2}\\&=f^{7}\end{aligned}$
For division, keep the base and subtract the indices rather than dividing them.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}f^{9}\div f^{3}\\&=f^{9-3}\\&=f^{6}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find $n$ in each equation: (a) $b^{4}\times b^{n}=b^{13}$; (b) $\frac{b^{n}}{b^{5}}=b^{8}$. Assume $b>0$ and $b\ne1$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Equal powers of this base have equal indices.
(a) Multiplication adds the indices.
$\begin{aligned}4+n&=13\\n&=13-4\\n&=9\end{aligned}$
(b) Division subtracts the indices.
$\begin{aligned}n-5&=8\\n&=8+5\\n&=13\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Write each expression as a single power: (a) $q^{3t+2}\times q^{2t-5}$; (b) $q^{4t+7}\div q^{t+3}$. Assume $q>0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Add the complete indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}q^{3t+2}\times q^{2t-5}\\&=q^{(3t+2)+(2t-5)}\\&=q^{5t-3}\end{aligned}$
(b) Subtract the complete denominator index.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}q^{4t+7}\div q^{t+3}\\&=q^{(4t+7)-(t+3)}\\&=q^{4t+7-t-3}\\&=q^{3t+4}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find $t$ if $a^{t}\times a^{3t}\times a^{4}=a^{28}$, where $a>0$ and $a\ne1$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Combine the powers by adding their indices.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}a^{t}\times a^{3t}\times a^{4}\\&=a^{t+3t+4}\\&=a^{4t+4}\end{aligned}$
Equal powers of this base have equal indices.
$\begin{aligned}4t+4&=28\\4t&=24\\t&=6\end{aligned}$

foundation.question_text: Write $x^{2}\times x^{5}$ as a single power.
Write $m\times m^{7}$ as a single power.
Write $b^{4}\times b^{2}\times b^{3}$ as a single power.
Explain why $x^{5}\times y^{2}$ cannot be written as a single power.
foundation.solution_text:
$x^{5}\times y^{2}$
The bases $x$ and $y$ are different, so no index law applies. The expression is already in its simplest form, $x^{5}y^{2}$.

foundation.question_text: Write $a^{7}\div a^{3}$ as a single power.
Simplify $\frac{x^{2}}{x^{6}}$, writing your answer in the form $\frac{1}{\text{base}^{n}}$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\frac{x^{2}}{x^{6}}$
The denominator has the higher power, so the base stays underneath.
$=\frac{1}{x^{6-2}}$
$=\frac{1}{x^{4}}$

foundation.question_text: For each expression, state whether you add or multiply the indices, then simplify: $\left(y^{4}\right)^{3}$ and $b^{4}\times b^{9}$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\left(y^{4}\right)^{3}$ is a power of a power, so multiply the indices.
$=y^{12}$
$b^{4}\times b^{9}$ is a product of the same base, so add the indices.
$=b^{13}$

development.question_text: Write $w^{5}\times w^{2}\times w^{3}\times w$ as a single power.
development.solution_text:
$w^{5}\times w^{2}\times w^{3}\times w$
$=w^{5}\times w^{2}\times w^{3}\times w^{1}$
$=w^{5+2+3+1}$
$=w^{11}$

$(x+3)^{7}\times (x+3)^{4}$
Both powers have the same base, $(x+3)$, so the indices add.
$=(x+3)^{7+4}$
$=(x+3)^{11}$

development.question_text: Explain why $\frac{g^{7}}{m^{4}}$ cannot be simplified using the index law of division.
development.solution_text:
$\frac{g^{7}}{m^{4}}$
The index law of division subtracts the indices of **matching** bases. Here the bases $g$ and $m$ are different, so there is nothing to cancel and the fraction stays as it is.

development.question_text: Simplify $\frac{q}{q^{9}}$, writing your answer in the form $\frac{1}{\text{base}^{n}}$.

development.solution_text:
$\frac{p^{15}}{p^{20}}$
The denominator has the higher power, so the base stays underneath.
$=\frac{1}{p^{5}}$
$\frac{p^{20}}{p^{15}}$
The numerator has the higher power, so the base stays on top.
$=p^{5}$

development.question_text: Write $\left(x^{2}\right)^{3}\times x^{4}$ as a single power.

Laura simplifies $e^{4}\times e^{3}$ and writes $e^{12}$.
Explain why she is incorrect and state the correct answer.
development.solution_text:
Laura multiplied the indices, but the power of a power law is the one that multiplies. Two powers of the same base being **multiplied** have their indices added.
$e^{4}\times e^{3}$
$=e^{4+3}$
$=e^{7}$

development.question_text:
A student writes $\frac{a^{7}}{a^{3}}=a^{\frac{7}{3}}$.
Explain the error and state the correct answer.
development.solution_text:
The student divided the indices, but the index law of division subtracts them — it is the bases that are being divided, not the indices.
$\frac{a^{7}}{a^{3}}$
$=a^{7-3}$
$=a^{4}$

mastery.question_text: Write $r^{2y+3}\times r^{y-2}$ as a single power.
Write $y^{2m+3}\div y^{m+5}$ as a single power.
Find the value of $x$ if $a^{x}\times a^{4x}\times a^{2}=a^{32}$, where $a>0$ and $a\ne1$.
mastery.solution_text:
$a^{x}\times a^{4x}\times a^{2}$
$=a^{x+4x+2}$
$=a^{5x+2}$
Since $a>0$ and $a\ne1$, equal powers of this base have equal indices.
$5x+2=32$
$5x=30$
$x=6$
